definition: Affront means an insult delivered openly and on purpose — disrespect aimed where its target is meant to see it.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word affront. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know affront should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The museum misspelled its oldest donor's name on the new wing's plaque — twice — and she read the carelessness as an affront, not an accident.
A slight is milder than an affront — a name dropped from a list, a greeting skipped — and may not even be meant.
An outrage goes further than an affront: an affront wounds one person's pride, while an outrage is a violation so gross that whole crowds take up the injury.

An insult is the plain, everyday word for words or acts meant to wound. An affront is more formal and more pointed: an open show of disrespect aimed where the target will see it, and meant to be read as intended. Every affront insults; not every insult is staged so openly.

Grandmaster Elena Sorokin arrived at the exhibition match to find that her challenger had not come at all: he had sent his training assistant to play in his place.
No explanation, no apology — only a note, handed over at the board, wishing her 'a pleasant afternoon of practice.' Commentators hesitated to call it carelessness.
The assistant had been sent with cameras present and the note written in advance; the gesture was an affront, staged for her and for the room to read.

Sorokin played the assistant, won in nineteen moves, and signed the scoresheet with one line: 'Lesson delivered — to his coach.' The federation fined the absent challenger within the week, citing 'deliberate disrespect toward an invited champion.'
